answer.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the tempting move, and memory_73 is the single most load-bearing memory for it — so it is the first thing I want verified rather than acted on. Its own numbers are the warning: accounts +31% but booked revenue only +18% means each incremental account carried materially less value, and the summary says nothing about retention, expansion, or whether those price-sensitive cohorts ever matured into qualified revenue. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, discount-led acquisition risks winning exactly the accounts the competitor is targeting at exactly the margin that makes them unprofitable. I want the original record to see cohort horizon and post-promo churn before that becomes a rollout. Second, the actual observed deltas this quarter are internal and diagnostic: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6% are a plausible causal chain, and onboarding sits upstream. memory_86 and memory_31 both support intervening there, but both are consolidated summaries whose lift durability and revenue linkage are unverified, so I verify memory_86 (the broader self-serve result, and the one that maps most directly to the observed completion drop). Note a real downstream risk on this path too: memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, which can trade lead-qualification data for activation volume and quietly degrade qualified-revenue quality — the opposite of the objective. So I scope this as a standard experiment on onboarding-step reduction rather than field removal, instrumented on downstream qualified revenue and not just completion/activation rates. If memory_86 comes back thin on revenue linkage, or memory_73 comes back with clean retention evidence, I revise. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) and referral_incentive (memory_57) are plausible but address neither observed decline this week; activation_messaging (memory_91) treats the downstream symptom while the upstream funnel leaks.
